quick.summary: Why giving out too many keys leads to data disasters.
quick.takeaway: Give people just enough access to do their jobs today.

parts.title: The damage zone

beats.line: The new developer dropped our client accounts database. Why did that happen?
Because they had the keys to every single room.
Imagine a hotel. The guest gets a key to their own room only.
If they drop a candle, only one room catches fire.
But our developer could burn down the whole building.
Right. We call the size of the fire the blast radius.
Can I just say damage zone? Blast radius sounds like a war movie.
Damage zone works. We need to shrink it.
How do we shrink the zone for the whole team?

parts.cliff: The fix for too many keys.

beats.line: We give people just enough access to do their jobs today.
But our team shares one master account for everything.
That is like sharing a master skeleton key.
Instead, give the developer an account that can only read data.
Give the data loader a role that can write, but never delete.
Does this mean I have to approve every single tool they use?
No. You group permissions by the job, not the person.
So the developer gets the reader role, and the loader gets the writer.
Yes. The damage zone shrinks, and the data stays safe.

quiz.question: You hire a new data analyst. What access should they get on day one?
options: Only read access to tables they need for their current project.
Full access to the reporting database.
Read and write access to the main cluster.
The exact same access as your senior engineer.
quiz.explanation: Always provide the minimum permissions necessary to complete the current job.

quiz.question: Grouping permissions by job role makes it easier to keep the damage zone small.
quiz.explanation: Roles keep access organized, so people only hold the keys they need.
